unique_units.replaces: Line Infantry (later replaces the Musketman-tier military unit chain)
unique_units.notes: An Industrial era melee unit with higher base Combat Strength and a large bonus fighting on the capital's home continent, plus Great General points from kills.

unique_infrastructure.name: Château
unique_infrastructure.notes: Must be built adjacent to a river and provides Culture, with bonus Culture the closer it is to a Wonder, reinforcing France's wonder-and-culture strategy.

leaders.historical_background: Catherine de' Medici (1519-1589) was an Italian-born queen consort and later regent of France during the tumultuous French Wars of Religion, wielding influence over her sons' reigns as king. She earned a fearsome reputation — fairly or not — for court intrigue, poison plots, and involvement in events like the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, cementing the 'Black Queen' legend that names her default in-game persona and its espionage/spy focus. Her family's Medici banking and political dynasty in Florence also connects to her later New Frontier persona, 'Magnificence,' which instead emphasizes courtly luxury and the collection of fine resources, echoing the opulent Medici court culture.

leaders.name: Wilfrid Laurier

leader_ability.name: The Last Best West
leader_ability.text: Canada can build Farms on Tundra tiles from the start of the game (and on Tundra Hills after Engineering), Mines/Lumber Mills on Tundra and Snow gain bonus Production, and Camps/Farms on those tiles gain bonus Food; flat Tundra/Snow and Tundra/Snow Hills tiles can also be purchased for less Gold, turning otherwise weak cold terrain into productive land.

agenda.name: Canadian Expeditionary Force
agenda.text: Laurier responds to World Congress Emergencies whenever possible and dislikes leaders who refuse to participate in Emergencies.

civ_ability.name: Four Faces of Peace
civ_ability.text: Canada cannot declare or be the target of Surprise Wars, and cannot declare war on city-states; it also gains Diplomatic Favor for accumulated Tourism and for completing Emergencies and Scored Competitions, making Canada a strongly diplomacy- and peace-oriented civilization.

unique_units.name: Mountie
unique_units.replaces: none (standalone Modern era light cavalry unit)
unique_units.notes: A low-maintenance cavalry unit that can found a National Park and gains a large Combat Strength bonus near National Parks (even more if Canadian-owned), primarily useful for defense rather than conquest.

unique_infrastructure.name: Ice Hockey Rink
unique_infrastructure.notes: Built on Tundra or Snow tiles, it grants Appeal, Amenities, Culture, and other bonuses to adjacent cold terrain, complementing Canada's tundra-focused kit.

leaders.historical_background: Sir Wilfrid Laurier (1841-1919) served as Canada's seventh Prime Minister from 1896 to 1911, presiding over a period of major western settlement and economic growth often summarized by his own phrase that the 20th century would 'belong to Canada.' He championed a policy of national unity between English and French Canadians and pursued a cautious, peace-oriented approach to Canada's relationship with the British Empire, reflected in the in-game civilization's inability to fight surprise wars or attack city-states. His government actively promoted immigration and settlement of the Canadian prairies and north, directly inspiring 'The Last Best West' ability's focus on making Tundra land productive.

leaders.name: Eleanor of Aquitaine
leaders.civilization: France or England (player's choice at game start)

leader_ability.name: Court of Love
leader_ability.text: Every Great Work present in one of Eleanor's cities exerts a cumulative -1 Loyalty per turn on foreign cities within 9 tiles; if a foreign city's Loyalty is driven to 0 while Eleanor is exerting the most pressure on it, that city peacefully defects and joins her civilization — enabling a non-military, culture-driven form of conquest.

agenda.name: Angevin Empire
agenda.text: Eleanor focuses on growing the Population of her own cities and dislikes leaders whose nearby cities have low Population, since low-population neighboring cities are easy prey for her Loyalty-pressure playstyle.

civ_ability.name: Uses the chosen civilization's ability
civ_ability.text: Eleanor is unique among Civ VI leaders in that the player chooses whether she leads France (gaining Grand Tour and France's unique units/infrastructure) or England (gaining England's civilization ability, currently 'Workshop of the World,' and units like the Sea Dog and Redcoat), while always keeping her own Court of Love leader ability and Angevin Empire agenda.

unique_units.name: Garde Impériale (if France)
unique_units.notes: Available if Eleanor is played as France; strong on the home continent with Great General points from kills.

unique_units.name: Sea Dog (if England)
unique_units.notes: Available if Eleanor is played as England; a strong naval raiding unit.

unique_units.name: Redcoat (if England)
unique_units.notes: Available if Eleanor is played as England; one of the strongest melee units through several eras, especially off the home continent.

unique_infrastructure.name: Château (if France)
unique_infrastructure.notes: River-adjacent Culture improvement, bonus near Wonders.

unique_infrastructure.name: Royal Navy Dockyard (if England)
unique_infrastructure.notes: England's Harbor replacement, boosting naval Production and strategic resource stockpiles.

leaders.historical_background: Eleanor of Aquitaine (c. 1122-1204) was one of medieval Europe's most powerful women, first as Queen of France through her marriage to Louis VII and later, after that marriage was annulled, as Queen of England through her marriage to Henry II — the basis for Civ VI's unusual choice to let players pick either civilization for her. She ruled vast territories in her own right as Duchess of Aquitaine, presided over a famously sophisticated court associated with the culture of courtly love (the namesake of her 'Court of Love' ability), and later backed her sons' rebellions against Henry II, spending years imprisoned as a result. Her personal patronage of troubadours, poets, and the arts across both French and English courts underlies her Great Works/Loyalty-pressure-based path to peacefully absorbing rival cities.

leaders.name: Peter

leader_ability.name: The Grand Embassy
leader_ability.text: When Russia has an active Trade Route to a civilization that is significantly more advanced in technology or civics, Peter gains bonus Science and Culture from that route (scaling with how far behind Russia is), incentivizing Russia to trade with — and catch up to — more advanced neighbors early on.

agenda.name: Westernizer
agenda.text: Peter is friendly toward civilizations that are ahead of him in technology and civics, and dislikes civilizations that are behind, reflecting his historical drive to modernize Russia along Western European lines.

civ_ability.name: Mother Russia
civ_ability.text: Russian cities claim extra surrounding territory the moment they are founded and gain bonus Faith and Production from Tundra tiles; in Gathering Storm, Russian units are also immune to Blizzard damage while enemies in Russian territory take extra Blizzard damage, letting Russia thrive in its characteristic cold, tundra-heavy homeland.

unique_units.name: Cossack
unique_units.notes: A strong Industrial era cavalry unit with bonus Combat Strength against wounded units, well-suited to finishing off weakened enemies.

unique_infrastructure.name: Lavra
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Holy Site at lower production cost; generates strong Great Prophet points (plus Great Writer/Artist/Musician points from its worship buildings) and expands the city's borders whenever a Great Person is activated there, making Russia excellent for religious and cultural strategies.

leaders.historical_background: Peter I ('Peter the Great', 1672-1725) ruled Russia (first as Tsar, later as Emperor) and pursued an aggressive campaign to modernize and Westernize the country, including a famous 1697-98 'Grand Embassy' tour of Western Europe — traveling incognito to study shipbuilding, military technology, and administration — that directly inspires his in-game leader ability and 'Westernizer' agenda. He founded St. Petersburg as a new, Western-facing capital, built Russia's first modern navy, and reformed the army, bureaucracy, and calendar. His reign's expansionist, cold-climate character (fighting the Great Northern War partly in harsh winter conditions) is echoed by Russia's tundra-friendly, territory-grabbing civilization ability.

leaders.name: Jayavarman VII

leader_ability.name: Monasteries of the King
leader_ability.text: Jayavarman's Holy Sites gain a strong adjacency bonus from Rivers, provide Housing when built on a River, generate Food equal to their total adjacency bonus, and trigger a Culture Bomb on nearby unowned tiles when built. This lets Khmer cities grow huge around river-adjacent Holy Sites while also expanding borders for free.

agenda.name: An End to Suffering
agenda.text: Jayavarman likes civilizations that build Holy Sites and maintain a high average city population, and dislikes those that neglect religion or keep small, undeveloped cities.

civ_ability.name: Grand Barays
civ_ability.text: Khmer Aqueducts grant bonus Faith and an Amenity in addition to their normal Housing bonus, and adjacent Farms receive extra Food, making Aqueduct placement a key part of Khmer city planning.

unique_units.name: Domrey
unique_units.notes: An elephant-mounted ballista that can move and fire in the same turn and exerts a zone of control, making it far more mobile and threatening than the siege unit it replaces.

unique_infrastructure.name: Prasat
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Temple, adds a Relic Great Work slot, and lets Missionaries killed in religious combat generate a Relic, tying nicely into a religious/culture hybrid strategy.

leaders.historical_background: Jayavarman VII (reigned c. 1181-1218) was the most powerful ruler of the Khmer Empire, expanding it to its greatest territorial extent from the capital of Angkor Thom in present-day Cambodia. A devout Mahayana Buddhist, he launched an unprecedented building program of temples, hospitals, roads, and reservoirs (barays), including the Bayon temple with its enormous carved stone faces. His combination of massive water-management infrastructure and prolific religious construction is directly reflected in the Khmer's in-game focus on Holy Sites, Aqueducts, and river-based city growth.

leaders.name: Saladin

leader_ability.name: Righteousness of the Faith
leader_ability.text: The worship building of Saladin's religion can be purchased by any civilization at a steep Faith discount, and it grants extra Science, Faith, and Culture to the cities that have it, letting Arabia's religion spread its economic benefits far beyond its own borders.

agenda.name: Ayyubid Dynasty
agenda.text: Saladin favors leaders who have adopted his religion's worship building and likes those who avoid war with its followers; he dislikes leaders who follow a different religion or attack civilizations that share his faith.

civ_ability.name: The Last Prophet
civ_ability.text: Arabia is guaranteed to receive the final available Great Prophet, virtually ensuring it can always found a religion, and it gains bonus Science for every foreign city following Arabia's religion.

unique_units.name: Mamluk
unique_units.notes: A heavy cavalry unit that heals every turn regardless of location, giving Arabian armies unusual staying power on extended campaigns.

unique_infrastructure.name: Madrasa
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the University with higher base Science and a Faith bonus equal to the city's Campus adjacency bonus, letting Arabia convert religious strength into science output.

leaders.historical_background: Saladin (Salah ad-Din, c. 1137-1193) was the Kurdish founder of the Ayyubid dynasty who unified Egypt and Syria under his rule and became the preeminent Muslim leader of the Crusades. He is best remembered for recapturing Jerusalem from the Crusader states in 1187 and for his chivalrous conduct toward defeated enemies, including Richard the Lionheart, which earned him a reputation for both military skill and honor across cultures. His deep association with founding and defending a shared faith across a wide territory underlies Arabia's in-game identity as the civilization most reliably able to found and spread a religion.

leaders.name: Gandhi

leader_ability.name: Satyagraha
leader_ability.text: For every civilization India has met that has founded a religion and is not at war with India, India gains bonus Faith; civilizations that go to war with India suffer an Amenities penalty, rewarding India for staying peaceful while religions spread around the world.

agenda.name: Peacekeeper
agenda.text: Gandhi avoids starting wars or actions that would brand him a warmonger, likes other leaders who keep the peace, and dislikes aggressive, war-prone civilizations.

civ_ability.name: Dharma
civ_ability.text: Indian cities gain the Follower Beliefs of every religion present within them rather than just the majority religion; from Gathering Storm onward India also gains an Amenity per religion present, extra Missionary spreads, and stronger religious pressure from Trade Routes, making India a religious-diversity powerhouse.

unique_units.name: Varu
unique_units.notes: A war-elephant unit that ignores enemy Zones of Control and reduces the combat strength of adjacent enemy units, making it a strong early anti-cavalry and area-denial unit.

unique_infrastructure.name: Stepwell
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement that provides Housing and Food, with bonus Food next to Farms and bonus Faith next to Holy Sites, supporting India's tall, high-population playstyle.

leaders.historical_background: Mohandas 'Mahatma' Gandhi (1869-1948) led India's independence movement from British colonial rule through a philosophy of nonviolent civil disobedience, or satyagraha ('truth-force'), that inspired later civil rights movements worldwide. A devout advocate of religious pluralism and tolerance between India's Hindu and Muslim communities, he was assassinated in 1948 shortly after independence was achieved. His commitment to nonviolence and interfaith coexistence is directly named in his leader ability (Satyagraha) and echoed in India's civilization ability, which rewards embracing many religions rather than enforcing one.

leaders.name: Menelik II

leader_ability.name: Council of Ministers
leader_ability.text: Ethiopian cities founded on Hills gain Science and Culture equal to a share of the Faith they generate, and Ethiopian units get a combat strength bonus when fighting on Hills, rewarding a hill-focused settling pattern.

agenda.name: Ethiopian Highlands
agenda.text: Menelik prefers to settle on Hills himself and likes civilizations that leave hill-heavy regions for Ethiopia to claim; he dislikes rivals who also aggressively settle Hills.

civ_ability.name: Aksumite Legacy
civ_ability.text: Ethiopian cities gain bonus Faith from resources, amplified further when international Trade Routes originate from resource-rich cities, and Ethiopia can purchase Archaeology Museums and Archaeologists with Faith.

unique_units.name: Oromo Cavalry
unique_units.notes: A light cavalry unit with improved Combat Strength and Sight that suffers no movement penalty on Hills, fitting Ethiopia's hill-based playstyle.

unique_infrastructure.name: Rock-Hewn Church
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement buildable only on Hills that generates strong Faith and cannot be destroyed by natural disasters, reinforcing Ethiopia's Faith-centric hill economy.

leaders.historical_background: Menelik II (reigned 1889-1913) was Emperor of Ethiopia who modernized the country's military and infrastructure while decisively defeating an invading Italian army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, preserving Ethiopian sovereignty during the era of European colonization of Africa. His reign built on centuries of Ethiopian Christian tradition, including the rock-hewn churches carved into hillsides at places like Lalibela centuries earlier, and expanded the empire's territory significantly. The in-game emphasis on Hills, Faith, and rock-hewn architecture directly reflects Ethiopia's highland geography and its long Christian religious heritage.

leaders.name: Gitarja

leader_ability.name: Exalted Goddess of the Three Worlds
leader_ability.text: Gitarja can purchase naval units with Faith and her religious units can embark and disembark for free, while City Centers adjacent to Coast or Lake tiles gain bonus Faith, tying Indonesia's naval and religious games together.

agenda.name: Archipelagic State
agenda.text: Gitarja favors civilizations that avoid settling or conquering cities on small, isolated landmasses and dislikes those with many such cities.

civ_ability.name: Great Nusantara
civ_ability.text: Coast and Lake tiles grant a minor adjacency bonus to Holy Sites, Campuses, Industrial Zones, and Theater Squares, and Entertainment Complexes gain extra Amenities, making coastal district placement especially rewarding for Indonesia.

unique_units.name: Jong
unique_units.notes: A unique naval ranged unit with higher movement than the Frigate it replaces, giving Indonesia strong early control of the seas.

unique_infrastructure.name: Kampung
unique_infrastructure.notes: A coastal tile improvement built adjacent to a water resource that grants Housing, Production, and Food scaling with adjacent Fishing Boats, supporting dense coastal cities.

leaders.historical_background: Gitarja (Dyah Gitarja, also known as Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, reigned 1328-1350) was a queen of the Majapahit Empire, one of the last and largest Hindu-Buddhist thalassocratic empires of maritime Southeast Asia, centered on Java. Under her rule and that of her son Hayam Wuruk, Majapahit extended influence across a vast archipelago through naval power and control of inter-island trade routes rather than contiguous land conquest. This archipelago-spanning, sea-based model of statecraft is the basis for Indonesia's in-game focus on coastal adjacency bonuses, naval units, and an agenda that rewards leaving small islands to Indonesia's control.

leaders.name: Jadwiga

leader_ability.name: Lithuanian Union
leader_ability.text: Foreign cities that lose territory to a Polish Culture Bomb convert to Poland's religion, and Jadwiga gains extra Gold, Culture, and Faith from Relics along with stronger Holy Site adjacency bonuses, blending Poland's territorial and religious games.

agenda.name: Saint
agenda.text: Jadwiga focuses on accumulating Faith and building up religion, and she favors other leaders who invest heavily in Faith generation.

civ_ability.name: Golden Liberty
civ_ability.text: Poland claims all surrounding unowned tiles whenever it builds an Encampment or Fort within its territory, and one of its government's Military policy slots becomes a flexible Wildcard slot, rewarding aggressive early border expansion.

unique_units.name: Winged Hussar
unique_units.notes: A powerful heavy cavalry unit that deals bonus damage and ignores Zone of Control when attacking damaged units, making it excellent at breaking through weakened enemy lines.

unique_infrastructure.name: Sukiennice
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Market and provides additional Gold and Great Merchant points, strengthening Poland's commercial output.

leaders.historical_background: Jadwiga (reigned 1384-1399) was crowned 'King' (rather than Queen, to underscore her full sovereign authority) of Poland at age ten, and her 1386 marriage to Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania created the Polish-Lithuanian union that grew into one of early modern Europe's largest states. A devoted patron of the Church, she funded the restoration of Kraków's university and pushed for the Christianization of pagan Lithuania. Her role in forging a lasting personal union between two realms is echoed in the leader ability's name, Lithuanian Union, while her religious patronage is reflected in her Faith-focused agenda and Relic bonuses.

leaders.name: Basil II

leader_ability.name: Porphyrogénnētos
leader_ability.text: Basil's heavy and light cavalry units deal full damage when attacking cities that follow the same religion as Byzantium, and researching Divine Right unlocks his powerful unique Tagma unit, rewarding a combined religious-military conquest strategy.

agenda.name: Divine Guardian
agenda.text: Basil II focuses on spreading his religion and defending it, favoring civilizations that share his faith and disliking those that follow a different one.

civ_ability.name: Taxis
civ_ability.text: Byzantine units gain bonus Combat and Religious Strength for every Holy City following Byzantium's religion (including its own), Byzantium's religion spreads automatically when an enemy unit is defeated in combat, and Holy Site cities earn extra Great Prophet points.

unique_units.name: Tagma
unique_units.notes: Unlocked via Basil's leader ability upon researching Divine Right; it grants Combat or Religious Strength to nearby friendly land units, functioning as a mobile support unit as well as a strong attacker.

unique_units.name: Dromon
unique_units.notes: A naval melee unit with greater range and combat strength than the Quadrireme, giving Byzantium an early naval edge.

unique_infrastructure.name: Hippodrome
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Entertainment Complex, costs less Production, grants extra Amenities, and spawns a free Heavy Cavalry unit each time the district or one of its buildings is completed.

leaders.historical_background: Basil II (reigned 976-1025) was one of the Byzantine Empire's most formidable emperors, expanding its borders to their greatest extent since Justinian through decades of relentless campaigning, most famously his prolonged conquest of the First Bulgarian Empire, which earned him the epithet 'Bulgar-Slayer.' Born 'porphyrogennetos' ('born in the purple'), meaning born to a reigning emperor in the palace's porphyry chamber, he ruled as a soldier-emperor who tied military success closely to Orthodox Christian identity and left the treasury and empire stronger than he found them. His fusion of religious authority with battlefield conquest is captured directly in his leader ability's name and its focus on converting military victories into religious dominance.

leaders.name: Philip II

leader_ability.name: El Escorial
leader_ability.text: Philip's Inquisitors gain an extra use of Remove Heresy, and his military and religious units gain a Combat or Religious Strength bonus against units belonging to civilizations that follow a different religion, rewarding religious uniformity backed by force.

agenda.name: Counter Reformer
agenda.text: Philip II wants every one of his cities to follow the same religion he does, favors civilizations that share his faith, and strongly dislikes anyone who spreads a different religion into his empire.

civ_ability.name: Treasure Fleet
civ_ability.text: Spain gains bonus yields from intercontinental Trade Routes and can form naval units into Fleets and Armadas earlier than other civilizations, reflecting Spain's historical dominance of transoceanic trade.

unique_units.name: Conquistador
unique_units.notes: A Renaissance-era unit that gains a large Combat Strength bonus when escorted by a religious unit and automatically converts captured cities to Spain's religion, combining conquest with religious conversion.

unique_infrastructure.name: Mission
unique_infrastructure.notes: A tile improvement providing Faith and Science, with extra yields when built adjacent to a Campus or on a continent other than Spain's home continent, rewarding overseas expansion.

leaders.historical_background: Philip II of Spain (reigned 1556-1598) ruled the largest empire the world had yet seen, spanning territories in Europe, the Americas, Africa, and Asia, funded in large part by silver shipped home in fleets from the New World. A fiercely devout Catholic monarch, he positioned himself as Europe's foremost defender of the Counter-Reformation, waging war against Protestant England and the Dutch rebels and overseeing the Spanish Inquisition's campaign against heresy. His combination of a religiously enforced empire and treasure-fleet-driven wealth is reflected directly in Spain's civilization ability and Philip's religious-conformity agenda and Inquisitor bonus.

leaders.name: Tamar

leader_ability.name: Glory of the World, Kingdom and Faith
leader_ability.text: Tamar gains Faith from combat victories based on the strength of the defeated unit, and after adopting Theology she can declare a special Protectorate War that doubles Faith output for a period and makes envoys sent to city-states that share Georgia's majority religion count double, tying military success to religious and diplomatic gains.

agenda.name: Narikala Fortress
agenda.text: Tamar fortifies her cities with the strongest available Walls and dislikes civilizations that leave their cities poorly defended.

civ_ability.name: Strength in Unity
civ_ability.text: Georgia earns bonus Era Score for Dedications made at the start of Golden and Heroic Ages and gains extra Production toward building Walls, helping it weather the Loyalty and warfare pressures of the Rise and Fall systems.

unique_units.name: Khevsur
unique_units.notes: A Medieval-era unit with a large Combat Strength bonus on Hills and no hill movement penalty, giving Georgia a strong defensive infantry option in its mountainous heartland.

unique_infrastructure.name: Tsikhe
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Renaissance-era City Center walls upgrade with substantially higher Outer Defense Strength plus bonus Faith and Tourism, reinforcing Georgia's fortress-focused playstyle.

leaders.historical_background: Tamar the Great (reigned 1184-1213) presided over the political, military, and cultural high point of the medieval Kingdom of Georgia, expanding its borders through successful campaigns while overseeing a flourishing of Georgian art, architecture, and literature, including the national epic 'The Knight in the Panther's Skin.' She ruled from heavily fortified strongholds carved into the Caucasus mountains, such as the Narikala fortress overlooking Tbilisi, defending her kingdom against Seljuk and other regional powers. Her reign's reputation for both formidable defenses and religious devotion (Georgia being one of the world's oldest Christian states) is reflected in her fortress-building agenda and Faith-generating combat ability.

leaders.name: Mansa Musa

leader_ability.name: Sahel Merchants
leader_ability.text: International Trade Routes gain bonus Gold for every flat Desert tile in their origin city, and entering a Golden or Heroic Age grants Mali a permanent extra Trade Route slot, rewarding a gold-focused desert trading empire.

agenda.name: Lord of the Mines
agenda.text: Mansa Musa single-mindedly pursues Gold accumulation and looks unfavorably on civilizations with weak Gold income.

civ_ability.name: Songs of the Jeli
civ_ability.text: Mali's City Centers gain extra Faith and Food for adjacent Desert and Desert Hills tiles, Commercial Hub buildings can be purchased with Faith, and Mines produce more Gold at the cost of reduced Production, in exchange for a Production penalty on units and buildings overall.

unique_units.name: Mandekalu Cavalry
unique_units.notes: A cavalry unit well-suited to protecting Mali's lucrative trade routes across the desert.

unique_infrastructure.name: Suguba
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Commercial Hub and provides discounts on Gold and Faith purchases made in its city, reinforcing Mali's wealth-and-Faith hybrid economy.

leaders.historical_background: Mansa Musa I (reigned c. 1312-1337) ruled the West African Mali Empire at the height of its wealth and power, controlling lucrative trans-Saharan trade routes in gold and salt. His 1324-1325 pilgrimage to Mecca became legendary for its extravagance—he reportedly distributed so much gold along the way that he temporarily depressed its value in the regions he passed through—cementing his reputation as perhaps the wealthiest individual in history. He also invested heavily in Islamic scholarship and architecture, transforming Timbuktu into a major center of learning. His singular association with fabulous gold wealth built on desert trade routes is the direct inspiration for his Gold-obsessed agenda and Mali's desert-and-trade-focused civilization ability.

leaders.name: Yongle

leader_ability.name: Lijia
leader_ability.text: Yongle's cities gain access to unique Lijia projects that convert a share of Production into Food, Faith, or Gold, and cities with high Population generate extra Gold, Science, and Culture per Citizen, rewarding large, well-developed Chinese cities.

agenda.name: Yinding
agenda.text: Yongle favors civilizations running a positive Gold income and dislikes those running a Gold deficit.

civ_ability.name: Dynastic Cycle
civ_ability.text: China's Eurekas and Inspirations provide a larger boost toward the cost of the technology or civic they unlock, and completing a Wonder grants a free Eureka and Inspiration, accelerating China's overall tech and civic progress.

unique_units.name: Crouching Tiger Cannon
unique_units.notes: An early gunpowder siege unit that does not require the Niter resource normally needed by the Bombard, letting China field powerful siege weapons without a strategic resource dependency.

unique_infrastructure.name: Great Wall
unique_infrastructure.notes: A unique tile improvement built on Hills that provides early defense and Gold, later converting to Culture and Tourism, and gains bonuses for connecting to adjacent Great Wall segments.

leaders.historical_background: The Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402-1424) was the third emperor of China's Ming dynasty, who seized the throne from his nephew and went on to relocate the capital to Beijing, where he commissioned the Forbidden City. He commissioned the enormous 'Yongle Encyclopedia' compiling China's accumulated knowledge, expanded and fortified sections of the Great Wall, and sponsored Admiral Zheng He's famous treasure-fleet voyages that projected Chinese naval power and trade across the Indian Ocean. Yongle is presented in Civilization VI as an alternate persona for China alongside the base game's Qin Shi Huang, added later via the Leader Pass DLC program, with his in-game focus on Production-conversion projects and large, wealthy cities reflecting his ambitious capital-building and encyclopedic era.

leaders.name: Dido

leader_ability.name: Founder of Carthage
leader_ability.text: Cities with a Cothon can use a unique project to relocate Phoenicia's capital there, and Dido gains extra Trade Route capacity and a Production bonus toward Districts in the city containing her Government Plaza, supporting a highly mobile, expansion-driven playstyle.

agenda.name: Sicilian Wars
agenda.text: Dido pursues coastal expansion for herself but dislikes rival civilizations that accumulate many coastal cities, echoing Carthage's historical rivalry with Greek colonies over Mediterranean coastlines.

civ_ability.name: Mediterranean Colonies
civ_ability.text: Coastal Phoenician cities founded on the same continent as the capital always have maximum Loyalty, embarked Settlers move faster and see farther with reduced embarkation costs, and Phoenicia starts with the Eureka for Writing already unlocked, making it exceptionally strong at rapid coastal settlement.

unique_units.name: Bireme
unique_units.notes: A faster, stronger naval melee unit that also shields nearby Traders from plundering, protecting Phoenicia's seaborne trade network.

unique_infrastructure.name: Cothon
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Harbor, boosts Production toward Settlers and naval units, heals naval units faster, and is required to relocate the Phoenician capital via Dido's leader ability.

leaders.historical_background: Dido is the legendary founder and first queen of Carthage, said in classical tradition (notably Virgil's Aeneid) to have fled Phoenician Tyre and founded her new city on the North African coast around the 9th century BC, growing it into one of the ancient Mediterranean's great maritime trading powers. Carthage's power rested on an extensive network of coastal colonies and trade routes stretching across the Mediterranean, a legacy that eventually put it in prolonged conflict with Greek city-states in Sicily and, later, with Rome in the Punic Wars. Her legendary founding of a new city by the sea and Phoenicia's historical mastery of coastal colonization directly shape both her capital-relocating leader ability and the civilization's emphasis on rapid, loyal coastal settlement.

leaders.name: Tokugawa

leader_ability.name: Bakuhan
leader_ability.text: Tokugawa's international Trade Routes suffer a penalty to all yields and Tourism, but his domestic Trade Routes grant bonus Culture, Science, and Gold for every specialty District at the destination, pushing Japan toward an inward-facing, isolationist economy built on strong domestic trade networks.

agenda.name: Sakoku
agenda.text: Tokugawa wants to remain safe from conquest, favoring civilizations that likewise avoid war and expansion by conquest, and he dislikes leaders who have captured other civilizations' capitals.

civ_ability.name: Meiji Restoration
civ_ability.text: Japanese Districts receive standard rather than reduced adjacency bonuses even when adjacency conditions would normally give a lesser bonus (such as on Hills or next to other districts), letting Japan cluster districts tightly for strong yields; cities near the capital also gain Amenities, with Tourism from Districts unlocked later after researching Flight.

unique_units.name: Samurai
unique_units.notes: A resilient melee unit that does not lose combat strength as it takes damage, letting it keep fighting effectively even when badly wounded.

unique_infrastructure.name: Electronics Factory
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the Factory and extends bonus Production and Culture to nearby cities rather than only its own city, strengthening Japan's tightly clustered industrial cities.

leaders.historical_background: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543-1616) was the daimyo who emerged victorious from Japan's chaotic Sengoku ('Warring States') period after his decisive victory at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that would rule Japan for over 250 years. His government pursued a policy of strict social order and, under his successors, near-total national seclusion (sakoku), closing Japan off from most foreign trade and contact to preserve internal stability. Added to Civilization VI as an alternate persona for Japan alongside the base game's Hojo Tokimune, his in-game penalty to foreign trade paired with strong domestic trade bonuses, along with an agenda built around avoiding conquest, directly mirrors the historical isolationist Sakoku policy associated with his dynasty.

leaders.name: Joao III

leader_ability.name: Porta do Cerco
leader_ability.text: All of João's units gain extra Sight, meeting a new civilization grants an additional Trade Route capacity, and Portugal automatically has Open Borders with all city-states, supporting an exploration-and-trade-focused playstyle from the earliest turns.

agenda.name: Navigator's Legacy
agenda.text: João III loves exploring the map and favors other civilizations that prioritize exploration as well.

civ_ability.name: Casa da Índia
civ_ability.text: Portuguese international Trade Routes can only target coastal cities or cities with a Harbor, but those routes gain a large yield bonus, and Portuguese Traders have increased range over water and can embark as soon as Trade Routes are unlocked, rewarding an ocean-spanning trade network.

unique_units.name: Nau
unique_units.notes: A naval unit with a free promotion and lower maintenance than the Caravel, and it carries charges to build the unique Feitoria improvement, linking exploration directly to Portugal's trade economy.

unique_infrastructure.name: Feitoria
unique_infrastructure.notes: Built only by a Nau on a foreign coastal city's tile next to a resource; Trade Routes sent to that city grant Portugal bonus Gold and Production, a unique way to profit from other civilizations' territory.

unique_infrastructure.name: Navigation School
unique_infrastructure.notes: Replaces the University and boosts Production toward naval units in its city, supporting Portugal's seafaring, exploration-heavy strategy.

leaders.historical_background: João III (reigned 1521-1557) ruled Portugal during the height of its overseas empire, consolidating and expanding the trading-post network established by his predecessors across the Atlantic, coastal Africa, India, and Southeast Asia through institutions like the Casa da Índia, which regulated the lucrative spice and goods trade with Portuguese Asia. His reign saw continued Portuguese exploration and colonization, including the beginnings of Portuguese Brazil's development, even as the crown increasingly relied on trade-post profits rather than large-scale territorial conquest. This coastal, trading-post-based model of empire—profit from controlled maritime trade routes rather than land conquest—is the direct basis for Portugal's Casa da Índia civilization ability and its unique Feitoria trading-post improvement.
